title: Labelling and Positive Identity
description: Call someone what you want them to be, and they often try to live up to it.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: Describing a person as the kind of person who does something — "you're a helpful neighbour" — increases the chance they will do it. The label becomes a small identity they want to be consistent with.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: People work to protect a positive self-image. A label creates an expectation, and behaving against it would create an uncomfortable inconsistency.

sections.title: Real-Life Examples
content: "You've always been generous with your time," said before a request for help.
A teacher telling a struggling pupil "you're the kind of student who works things out" before a hard task.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: A flattering trait named just before an ask.
A person described as already being what the persuader wants.

sections.title: Ethical Uses
sections.content: Naming a genuine strength honestly encourages people to act on the best version of themselves.

sections.title: Manipulative Uses
sections.content: Praising a trait you do not believe they have, purely to trigger the discomfort of refusing.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: Flattery that arrives exactly alongside a request.
A label you do not actually recognise in yourself.

sections.title: Defense Strategies
content: Separate the compliment from the ask; you can accept one and decline the other.
Ask whether the label is accurate.

sections.title: Mistakes People Make
content: Feeling obliged to prove a flattering label true.
Missing that the praise was instrumental.

sections.title: Key Lessons
content: You can decline a request without rejecting a compliment.
